questions.q: Write the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃. Identify whether it is a primary, secondary, or tertiary haloalkane.
questions.a: 2-Chlorobutane; secondary haloalkane. The parent chain is butane (4 carbons). Numbering from the end nearer to Cl gives locant 2. The carbon bearing Cl is attached to two other carbons (CH₃ and CH₂CH₃), making it secondary. A wrong answer like "1-chlorobutane" reveals the student numbered from the wrong end. "Chlorobutane" without locant reveals ignorance of the lowest locant rule. "Butyl chloride" reveals reliance on common names instead of IUPAC.

questions.q: Explain why the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCl is chloroethene and not vinyl chloride, and why the carbon bearing Cl is sp² hybridised.
questions.a: Chloroethene follows IUPAC: parent = ethene (2-carbon chain with double bond), halogen prefix = chloro at C-1. "Vinyl chloride" is a common name. The carbon bearing Cl is part of C=C, so it is sp² hybridised (trigonal planar, 120°). A student writing "chloroethane" misses the double bond. Writing "1-chloroethene" is redundant (locant 1 is implied for terminal double bond). Confusing sp² with sp³ reveals misunderstanding of hybridisation's role in classification (vinylic vs alkyl halide).

questions.q: Draw the structure and give the IUPAC name for the compound with molecular formula C₄H₈Br₂ that has both bromine atoms on the same carbon.
questions.a: Structure: CH₃CH₂CBr₂CH₃ (or CH₃CBr₂CH₂CH₃). IUPAC name: 2,2-dibromobutane. Parent = butane (4 carbons). Both Br on C-2 → "2,2-dibromo". A student drawing CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃ (2,3-dibromobutane) confuses geminal (same carbon) with vicinal (adjacent carbons). Writing "dibromobutane" without locants violates the lowest locant rule. Naming it "butane-2,2-dibromide" uses incorrect suffix style (halogens are prefixes, not suffixes).

questions.q: Compare the IUPAC naming of 1-bromo-2-methylbenzene and 1-bromo-3-methylbenzene. Why does the common name system use "o-" and "m-" while IUPAC uses numbers?
questions.a: 1-Bromo-2-methylbenzene (ortho) and 1-bromo-3-methylbenzene (meta) have the same substituents but different relative positions on the benzene ring. IUPAC uses numbers (1,2 and 1,3) because they are unambiguous for all substitution patterns, including tri- and higher-substituted benzenes where o/m/p fail. Common names o-/m-/p- only work for disubstituted benzenes. A student saying "o-bromotoluene" for the first is using common name, not IUPAC. Writing "2-bromo-1-methylbenzene" violates alphabetical order (bromo before methyl) and lowest locant set (1,2 vs 2,1 — same set, but alphabetical decides numbering direction).

questions.q: A student writes the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br as "1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane". Evaluate if this is correct. If not, give the correct name and explain the error.
questions.a: Correct. Parent chain = propane (3 carbons: C-CH₂-Br with two CH₃ on C-2). Numbering from Br end gives Br at C-1, two methyls at C-2 → 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane. Common error: choosing butane chain (CH₃)₃C-CH₂Br as 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylbutane — wrong because longest chain is 3 carbons (the neopentyl system). Another error: "neopentyl bromide" (common name). The student must identify the longest continuous chain, not the total carbons.

questions.q: Design a set of three structural isomers with formula C₅H₁₁Cl, name each by IUPAC, and classify each as primary, secondary, or tertiary. Explain your reasoning for the parent chain selection in each.
questions.a:
1. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl → 1-chloropentane (1°). Parent = pentane (5C straight chain). Cl on terminal C.
2. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(Cl)CH₃ → 2-chloropentane (2°). Parent = pentane. Cl on C-2 (attached to 2 carbons).
3. (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl → 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane (1°). Parent = propane (longest chain = 3C). Cl on primary CH₂.
Other valid isomers: 3-chloropentane (2°), 1-chloro-3-methylbutane (1°), 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (2°), 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (3°). A poor answer misses isomers, misclassifies, or picks wrong parent chain (e.g., calling isomer 3 "neopentyl chloride" without IUPAC).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ of haloalkanes and haloarenes is the systematic IUPAC naming of organic compounds where one or more hydrogen atoms of aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbons are replaced by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I), following the "haloalkane" (alkyl halide) and "haloarene" (aryl halide) naming conventions with locants for halogen position and substituents.
Fill in the blank: Look at a medicine strip — many drugs like chloramphenicol (antibiotic) or halothane (anaesthetic) contain halogen atoms ______ to carbon chains or rings.
What is Nomenclature of haloalkanes and haloarenes? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Nomenclature of haloalkanes and haloarenes is the systematic IUPAC naming of organic compounds where one or more hydrogen atoms of aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbons are replaced by halogen atoms (F, Cl, Br, I), following the "haloalkane" (alkyl halide) and "haloarene" (aryl halide) naming conventions with locants for halogen position.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Nomenclature of haloalkanes and haloarenes?
questions.a: Students frequently choose the parent chain based on total carbon count rather than the longest continuous chain.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can correctly write the IUPAC name from a given structure and draw the structure from a given IUPAC name for mono-, di-, and polyhalogenated alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, cycloalkanes, and arenes, including correct use of prefixes (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo), locants, and stereochemical descriptors where applicable.
